title: Funeral boss 'The Undertaker' seen in police surveillance amid Toronto mafia probe
summary: Police records obtained by CBC News show Toronto-area funeral home president Luigi Vescio Sr. has been on the radar of Canadian and Italian investigators for nearly a decade. He and his family…

image.caption: Luigi Vescio Sr. is seen in a promotional video released by his limousine firm, and in 2019 police surveillance images. (Phantom Limousine Service; York Regional Police)

blocks.text: Toronto·CBC Investigates

Police records obtained by CBC News show Toronto-area funeral home president Luigi Vescio Sr. has been on the radar of Canadian and Italian investigators for nearly a decade. He and his family business were sanctioned by the U.S. last week amid allegations Vescio played a “senior” role in the mob.
Luigi Vescio Sr., sanctioned for alleged ties to 'Ndrangheta syndicate, has been on police radar since 2019
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 26, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 2 hours ago

When the U.S. slapped financial sanctions on a family-owned chain of Toronto-area funeral homes last week — alleging the company's president played a "senior" role in the Italian mob — the dramatic move likely surprised some clients.
But police records obtained by CBC News show Luigi (Lui) Vescio Sr. has been on the radar of Canadian and Italian investigators for nearly a decade.

Police in Ontario captured surveillance images of Vescio meeting in 2019 with visitors from Italy — purportedly leading figures in the notorious Calabrian criminal syndicate known as the 'Ndrangheta. Months later, Italian authorities sought his arrest on a charge of mafia association.

A news release issued last week by the U.S. Treasury Department identified Vescio, 55, as a key player in the criminal group's Canadian wing. The statement said the 'Ndrangheta in the Toronto area has "strengthened in recent years, becoming so powerful that they dictate events in Italy from across the ocean."

From left, Luigi Vescio Sr., his wife Rose and their children Laura and Luigi Jr. All four were recently sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department over alleged ties to the Italian criminal syndicate known as the 'Ndrangheta. (Vescio Funeral Homes)

The Treasury Department said the 'Ndrangheta in Canada is involved in drug trafficking, money laundering and murder. It named five other men reported to be leaders of the group in the Toronto area, including the purported top boss, Angelo (Don Angelino) Figliomeni.

The statement did not specify how the Canadian-born Vescio's businesses are suspected of fitting into the alleged conspiracy. One location in Vaughan, Ont., came into the spotlight in 2019 for hosting a Hells Angels funeral, attended by bikers from across the country.

Washington also sanctioned Vescio's wife Rose and their adult children Luigi Jr. and Laura "for acting on behalf" of Luigi Sr., who is also known as "The Undertaker." All three family members are listed as owners of Vescio Funeral Homes' three locations in the Toronto area, while Luigi Sr. serves as president.
The Vescio Funeral Home in the Maple district of Vaughan, Ont., north of Toronto. (Pelin Sidki/CBC)
The Vescios and their company did not respond to requests for comment. The allegations against them have not been tested in a Canadian court and the U.S. did not provide evidence for its findings.
No one answered when a reporter knocked on the door of the family's Vaughan home. Signs posted in front of the light brown brick house warned of cane corso dogs "on duty."

In a brief interview posted on social media last year, a smiling Vescio — who has tattoos covering his head and neck — said "we own service-oriented businesses," including the funeral homes and a limousine rental firm.
"I started [in the industry] when I was 15, and still pluggin' away," he said in the interview.

blocks.text: Pictured during surveillance operation

According to Italian police files and York Regional Police intelligence reports reviewed by CBC News, Vescio was seen picking up high-ranking Italian mob figure Vincenzo Muià at Toronto Pearson Airport on March 31, 2019.

Muià had travelled from Italy to confront other figures about the 2018 ambush killing of his brother in Siderno, Calabria, and to apparently seek permission to strike back against those he believed were responsible, the files say.
Luigi Vescio Sr. is seen in a 2019 police surveillance image, carrying a brown envelope outside one of his family's funeral homes. (York Regional Police)

Police noted that during his two-week visit, Muià stayed at the Vescios' five-bedroom home, which has a wine cellar, an in-ground pool and a black-and-white portrait from the movie The Godfather hanging in the den.
Records show investigators kept a close eye on Muià and his associates, including Vescio, during the trip.

blocks.text: A York police photo included in the surveillance report shows Vescio holding a brown envelope in the parking lot of one of his Vaughan funeral homes. In a separate image, he's seen with Muià and other suspected mob figures outside an Italian restaurant in Toronto.

Luigi Vescio Sr., far right, is seen with other men observed in a police surveillance operation in the spring of 2019. York Regional Police captured images of Italian mob figure Vincenzo Muià and his associates during his two-week visit to the Toronto area. (York Regional Police)

Italian authorities even managed to listen surreptitiously to Muià's conversations with Vescio and others after bugging the Italian's mobile phone — effectively providing them with a live microphone by his side at all times.
The eavesdropping became a key sticking point in Canada's efforts to deport Vincenzo (Jimmy) DeMaria, another one of the purported 'Ndrangheta leaders now facing U.S. sanctions.
Long investigation into alleged Italian mobster could collapse
That came after Project Sindacato, a multimillion-dollar York police probe targeting the 'Ndrangheta, collapsed in 2021 following accusations that investigators illegally intercepted phone calls.
What do the sanctions mean?

The Trump administration moved to sanction 'Ndrangheta members last week because it said the organization provided "essential logistical and operational support" for major Mexican drug cartels, which the U.S. and Canada classify as terrorist groups.

The sanctions ensure the Vescios and their firms can't deal directly with U.S. banks or clients. In effect, it will mean they'll also be cut off from Canadian financial institutions, said Jessica Davis, president of Ottawa-based Insight Threat Intelligence.

"Because of the inter-linkages between the Canadian and U.S. financial systems, any Canadian financial institution doing business with those sanctioned entities is now going to look at them and say, 'your risk rating has really escalated,'" Davis said.
Staff at the funeral homes told callers on Monday that it's "business as usual," while avoiding talk of the ongoing turmoil.

Vincenzo (Jimmy) DeMaria, left, and Angelo (Don Angelino) Figliomeni are among several individuals and firms sanctioned in Canada by the U.S. Treasury Department, amid allegations they hold leading roles in the Toronto-area branch of the 'Ndrangheta. (U.S. Treasury Department)
By Tuesday, however, there were signs of trouble. Employees answering the phones at two locations confirmed the funeral homes could not process card payments.
Davis, a former CSIS analyst, said unless it can operate as a cash-only business, it's likely any such sanctioned entity would be forced to close.

blocks.text: The Bereavement Authority of Ontario, the funeral industry regulator, declined to comment directly on Vescio Funeral Homes, but said families can reach out if they have concerns about prepaid arrangements.
"All prepaid funds for arrangements are held within a third-party trust fund," spokesperson David Brazeau told CBC News in an email.
Both the RCMP and York police — which the Treasury Department said helped in the sanctions case — declined to comment directly on the Vescios or the sanctions.
